question: Can multi-grade deep learning overcome the low-frequency training bias of an end-to-end ReLU network by fitting successive residuals with shallow modules composed through frozen features, while retaining comparable architecture size and practical training time on oscillatory functions, coordinate images, and modified MNIST regression?

key_findings.claim: The strongest result is a large and visually credible optimization advantage over the paper's end-to-end ReLU baseline on its deterministic sinusoid benchmarks.
key_findings.evidence: Across four one-dimensional sums containing frequencies 10 through 200, MGDL reports test RSE from 1.7e-5 to 1.3e-3 versus 0.12 to 0.77 for SGDL, improvements of 592 to 7,058 times, with reported wall times no larger than SGDL. The manifold experiment up to frequency 400 shows similarly large gaps in its difficult q=0 and q=4 cases. Original-resolution inspection of Figures 2, 4, 8, and 10 confirms that later-grade input-to-output contributions contain the missing high-frequency magnitudes. These results establish that the sequential frozen-feature/residual procedure can be much easier to optimize than one particular deep ReLU training setup, even though they do not isolate why.

key_findings.claim: MGDL does not explicitly decompose the target into frequency bands, so the paper's frequency-specific mechanism is inferred rather than enforced.
key_findings.evidence: At each grade the method minimizes ordinary MSE on the entire current residual using an unconstrained ReLU shallow network composed with frozen preceding hidden maps. There is no Fourier-domain loss, band-pass filter, spectral allocation, frequency constraint, or rule assigning a grade to a band. The later-grade contributions happen to shift upward in frequency in these examples, but the algorithm is generic greedy residual fitting and could learn any component that reduces MSE. The text's stated decomposition into different frequency components is therefore a post-hoc interpretation rather than the optimization problem actually solved.

key_findings.claim: The spectral plots do not demonstrate that each newly trained shallow module is itself low-frequency in the coordinates on which it is trained.
key_findings.evidence: The paper plots each grade's final contribution as a function of the original input: for grade j this is the newly learned shallow output after composition with all frozen hidden maps. Those displayed functions contain progressively higher original-coordinate frequencies. No spectrum is shown for the new shallow module as a function of its internal feature vector, where Fourier frequency is not even uniquely defined without a coordinate convention. Thus the figures support progressive recovery of final signal components, but not the central assertion that every SNN only learns a low-frequency function and composition alone creates the high frequencies.

anchors.section: Figure 2 and definitions of N_j and H_j
Claim that each grade focuses solely on a low-frequency component

key_findings.claim: The Jacobi-Anger motivation is an existence example, not a representation or optimization theory for MGDL.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 4-5 correctly show that composing a cosine with a sinusoid can generate harmonics. But this does not show that an arbitrary target has an efficient sum-of-compositions of low-frequency functions, that such factors are representable at the stated widths, or that greedy Adam training recovers them. Equation 3 is presented as a specially constructed illustrative function whose factors are not analytically specified in the paper. The conclusion itself acknowledges that a theoretical foundation for MGDL's spectral-bias claim is absent.

key_findings.claim: The only theorem is a near-tautological monotone training-residual result under exact grade-wise optimization, not a spectral-bias, convergence, or generalization guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 states that the optimal MSE residual strictly decreases when the next learned grade contribution is nonzero. Because the next hypothesis class can choose the zero contribution and is assumed to be optimized, non-increase follows directly; strict decrease is conditional on the selected contribution. The theorem gives no frequency localization, approximation rate, finite-iteration optimizer result, validation behavior, generalization bound, or advantage over end-to-end training. The statement that all numerical examples 'validate' it adds little because every nontrivial residual fit should reduce its own training loss.

key_findings.claim: The experiment does not isolate sum-composition from repeated residual fitting, restarts, frozen-feature conditioning, or a larger sequential optimization budget.
key_findings.evidence: SGDL receives K epochs once, whereas every one of four or five MGDL grades receives K epochs, so MGDL performs four or five separately initialized optimization stages and repeated passes over the residual data. Shallow backpropagation makes reported wall time competitive on the synthetic and manifold tasks, which is a legitimate efficiency result, but equal wall time does not identify the causal mechanism. Missing ablations include a sum of independent shallow residual learners without feature composition, frozen compositions without residual summation, stage-wise training followed by end-to-end fine-tuning, deep supervision, equal optimizer updates/FLOPs, and restart-matched SGDL.

key_findings.claim: The competitive evaluation is far too narrow to establish that MGDL solves spectral bias relative to the field.
key_findings.evidence: Every table compares only MGDL with an end-to-end ReLU network of the same nominal depth and width. The paper cites PhaseDNN, adaptive activations, MscaleDNN, and Fourier features but implements none of them, even for coordinate-image regression where Fourier features are a direct published baseline. It also omits SIREN, multiplicative filter networks, BACON, WIRE, DINER, FINER, Fourier-reparameterized INRs, and normalization-based coordinate networks. Therefore the paper supports an SGDL-versus-MGDL result, not superiority over established high-frequency representations.

key_findings.claim: The image-regression evaluation leaks training pixels into its test metric and appears to tune hyperparameters on the same full image.
key_findings.evidence: The training grid contains every other row and column, one quarter of the pixels, while the reported test set contains all pixels; hence every training pixel is included in TePSNR. There is no held-out-only PSNR or validation image subset. Appendix B says optimal image parameters were selected by the highest PSNR, without defining a training-only selection metric, while Table 3 and the captions emphasize testing PSNR. The released code constructs the training coordinates as test_x[::2,::2] and evaluates on the full grid. This contamination and ambiguous model selection prevent interpreting the 2.35-3.93 dB gains as clean interpolation generalization.

anchors.section: Section 3.3 train and test pixel definitions

key_findings.claim: Table 3 reports per-grade rather than cumulative MGDL time, obscuring that Cat is nearly twice as slow as SGDL and the other image cases are only approximately tied.
key_findings.evidence: The table lists separate times for grades 1-4. Summing them gives 146 seconds for Cat versus 77 for SGDL, 689 versus 685 for Sea, and 716 versus 742 for Building. Reading the final-grade row alone as total time would incorrectly report 28, 182, and 182 seconds. The paper does not print these cumulative comparisons next to its quality claims.

anchors.section: Claim that training time grows linearly with grades

key_findings.claim: The modified-MNIST experiment measures robustness to oscillatory label corruption, not successful learning of a high-frequency target.
key_findings.evidence: Training and validation targets multiply the one-hot label by 1+beta sin(2 pi kappa ||x||), but testing uses the clean one-hot label. MGDL wins by fitting the corrupted training targets less well: at beta=1 its TrRSE is about 0.35 versus 0.30-0.31 for SGDL, while its clean-test RSE is 0.078-0.080 versus 0.10-0.11. That is evidence of implicit regularization or underfitting the high-frequency label term, not of capturing it. For beta greater than one the multiplier can be negative, reversing the correct class's target sign, and no classification accuracy, calibration, or clean-trained control is reported.

key_findings.claim: The MNIST evidence is not frequency-specific and the supporting figures contain legend inconsistencies.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 is virtually invariant across kappa=1, 5, 10, and 50 for both methods, which does not show a dependence on the injected frequency. The one-hot classifier tau_0 is piecewise constant on an uncharacterized image manifold and is itself not established to be low-frequency in ambient Euclidean coordinates. At original resolution, Figures 14-15 duplicate each kappa label for training and validation curves and do not visibly include kappa=50 despite the stated sweep through 50. These plots cannot support the claimed broad high-dimensional frequency conclusion.

anchors.section: Definition of tau_0 and radial modulation

key_findings.claim: The normalized spectral heatmaps discard phase and clip overshoot, so their brightest cells do not mean accurate Fourier recovery.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B defines each heatmap value as learned amplitude divided by target amplitude and clips the colorbar to [0,1]. Ratios above one are therefore rendered identically to the ideal ratio one, and amplitude alone ignores phase error. Zero-extending a function defined on [0,1] also introduces boundary-dependent spectral leakage. The scalar RSE tables are more informative than Figures 9-10, but those heatmaps should not be read as direct accuracy maps.

anchors.section: Appendix B.1 heatmap normalization and clipping

key_findings.claim: The claimed manifold injectivity and dimension-independence are not established by the experiments.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 10 is called an injective map from the closed interval [0,1], but gamma_q(0)=gamma_q(1), so it is not injective on that domain; the chosen targets are periodic enough that the endpoint collision is harmless here. The only high-dimensional input is 784-dimensional MNIST with dense layers, and its result is label-noise robustness rather than faithful oscillatory regression. There is no input-dimension sweep, memory/compute scaling, or comparable task across dimensions, so the conclusion that the approach is 'not limited by dimension' exceeds the evidence.

key_findings.claim: Results are reported from effectively one deterministic seed without uncertainty or statistical testing.
key_findings.evidence: Synthetic phases, validation coordinates, and test coordinates use fixed seeds, and the released initialization path resets NumPy's seed. No experiment reports repeated initializations, mean and standard deviation, confidence interval, or a paired significance analysis. The large synthetic gaps are unlikely to vanish solely from seed variation, but the absence of distributions prevents assessing stability, hyperparameter-selection variance, and the smaller image/MNIST gains.

key_findings.claim: Code is publicly linked, but the current repository is not an executable or archival reproduction package.
key_findings.evidence: The linked GitHub repository contains separate SGDL/MGDL scripts and input images for all four tasks, so code availability is real. However, it has no license, dependency manifest or lockfile, tests, CI, checkpoints, raw metric tables, or result directories. Analysis scripts contain an author-specific absolute environment path. The current synthetic MGDL entrypoint passes undefined lambda_W after defining lambd_W; the MNIST MGDL entrypoint uses undefined nn_parameter and mul_lambd_W. Default epochs also diverge sharply from the paper: MNIST SGDL uses 30 instead of 2,000, image MGDL 200 per grade instead of 10,000, and manifold scripts 300 instead of 30,000. Syntax compilation succeeds, but literal runtime reproduction requires code fixes, environment reconstruction, and manual restoration of paper configurations.

method.core_idea: Replace end-to-end optimization of a deep ReLU network with a sequence of shallow residual-learning grades. Freeze the hidden maps learned in earlier grades, compose them into the next grade's feature input, and sum every grade's output so later shallow optimizations can recover components that are difficult for a jointly trained deep model.
method.mechanism: Split a depth-D network into L shallow networks. Grade 1 fits the target by MSE. At grade l, recursively compute features by applying all frozen earlier hidden maps, form the residual after subtracting previous grade outputs, and train a new shallow output network on those feature-residual pairs. The final predictor is the sum of the input-to-output contribution from every grade. Use ReLU, Xavier initialization, and Adam with fixed or exponentially decaying learning rates. Interpret the progression through grades using Fourier amplitudes of each final contribution and compare with a same-width, same-total-depth ReLU network trained end to end.
assumptions: High-frequency targets admit useful low-complexity sum-of-compositions decompositions.
A newly trained shallow module learns a low-frequency function in its internal feature coordinates even when its composed original-coordinate output is high-frequency.
Greedy MSE residual minimization discovers the intended decomposition without explicit spectral constraints.
Freezing earlier features does not prevent later grades from correcting representation errors that require changes to those features.
Same nominal total depth and width make SGDL and MGDL comparable despite different optimization schedules and effective parameter-use patterns.
Comparable wall time is an adequate compute control even when MGDL performs four or five times as many epoch stages.
A single fixed initialization/data seed represents method-level performance.
Uniformly sampled synthetic test coordinates measure generalization rather than interpolation of a dense deterministic grid.
Zero-extended Fourier amplitudes on [0,1] faithfully characterize the relevant notion of spectral bias.
Amplitude-ratio heatmaps remain meaningful without phase and after clipping values above one.
Full-image PSNR is a valid test metric despite including the quarter-grid training pixels.
Image hyperparameters can be selected by highest PSNR without a separately defined validation set.
Generalization to clean MNIST labels after training on radial label modulation measures the ability to learn high-frequency features.
One 784-dimensional task is enough to support input-dimension independence.
The released repository and commented paper configurations are sufficient to reconstruct the reported runs despite broken current entrypoints and absent environments/results.

techniques.role: Train a deep computation incrementally as shallow frozen-feature grades.
Make each new grade regress the target residual left by earlier grades.
Reuse compositions of earlier hidden maps without updating their parameters.
Sum contributions whose shallow output modules are composed with successively deeper frozen maps.
Inspect one-sided amplitude spectra and their evolution across training grades.
Represent RGB images as functions mapping two-dimensional coordinates to color.
Multiply MNIST one-hot targets by a radial sinusoid to create oscillatory label corruption.
Inspect all nineteen pages, equations, four tables, Figures 1-15, captions, axes, legends, and heatmap scales at original resolution.
Inspect the official TeX/figure archive and the linked GitHub implementation at an immutable commit.
Compare the claims with direct spectral-bias and implicit-representation methods through August 2026.

evaluations.setting: Four one-dimensional synthetic functions on [0,1], each summing 20 sinusoids at frequencies 10, 20, ..., 200 with four amplitude schedules; 6,000 grid training points and 2,000 random validation/test points.
evaluations.metric: Training, validation, and test relative squared error; wall time; one-sided Fourier magnitude plots.
evaluations.result: MGDL test RSE is 1.7e-5, 6.5e-6, 2.1e-5, and 1.3e-3 versus SGDL's 0.12, 5.7e-3, 0.11, and 0.77, with reported times of 9,875-27,817 seconds versus 31,808-41,063. This is strong evidence against the chosen end-to-end baseline, but only one fixed-seed protocol and no modern spectral baseline are tested.
evaluations.baseline: Eight-layer SGDL for settings 1-3 and ten-layer SGDL for setting 4, compared with four- or five-grade MGDL of the same nominal total hidden depth and width.

evaluations.setting: Regression on flower curves or a unit circle embedded in R2, with targets containing 40 sinusoidal components at frequencies through 400; 12,000 grid training points and 4,000 random validation/test points.
evaluations.metric: Relative squared error, wall time, per-grade spectra, and spectrum-evolution heatmaps.
evaluations.result: For hard cases, MGDL lowers test RSE from 0.28 or 0.54 to about 1e-4-2e-4 and from 0.01 to 8.7e-5 while using less reported time. The map is incorrectly called injective on [0,1], the heatmaps clip overshoot, and no alternative INR or multi-scale baseline is included.
evaluations.baseline: One eight-layer end-to-end ReLU SGDL network.

evaluations.setting: Coordinate regression for Cat, Sea, and Building RGB images, training on every other row and column and evaluating on the entire image grid.
evaluations.metric: Training and full-grid PSNR plus per-grade wall time and reconstructed images.
evaluations.result: Four-grade MGDL improves the reported full-grid PSNR by 2.35, 3.93, and 2.88 dB. However, the metric includes all training pixels, no held-out-only or validation PSNR is provided, hyperparameter selection is ambiguous, and cumulative MGDL times are 146, 689, and 716 seconds versus SGDL's 77, 685, and 742.
evaluations.baseline: One twelve-layer end-to-end ReLU SGDL coordinate network; Fourier features and other direct image-INR baselines are omitted.

evaluations.setting: MNIST vector regression with 45,000 training and 15,000 validation samples whose one-hot labels are multiplied by 1+beta sin(2 pi kappa ||x||), then evaluation on 10,000 clean one-hot test labels.
evaluations.metric: Training/validation loss and training, validation, and clean-test relative squared error.
evaluations.result: At beta=1, three-grade MGDL has worse corrupted-training RSE (about 0.35 versus 0.30-0.31) but lower clean-test RSE (0.078-0.080 versus 0.10-0.11), a 27-29% improvement that is almost invariant across kappa. This demonstrates robustness or implicit regularization against label modulation, not faithful high-frequency learning.
evaluations.baseline: One six-layer end-to-end ReLU SGDL regressor; no clean-trained control or classification metric.

open_questions: Does MGDL still outperform Fourier features, SIREN, MFN, BACON, WIRE, FINER, and CAFE under matched parameters, FLOPs, optimizer updates, and wall time?
What definition of frequency applies to a shallow module acting on a learned multivariate feature coordinate?
Can any theorem connect grade-wise feature composition to a target's Fourier spectrum or spectral convergence rate?
How often does greedy residual learning discover a compact sum-of-compositions when such a decomposition exists?
Which gains remain after comparing with an independent shallow residual ensemble that omits frozen-feature composition?
Do end-to-end fine-tuning, block-coordinate training, deep supervision, or matched restarts close the SGDL gap?
How do results change under equal total optimizer updates and measured FLOPs rather than equal epochs per stage?
How stable are results across initialization, sample, phase, and hyperparameter-selection seeds?
Does MGDL improve true held-out-pixel PSNR when training pixels are excluded and tuning uses a separate validation grid?
Does MGDL preserve its image advantage against direct Fourier-feature and periodic-activation coordinate networks?
On MNIST, what happens to clean and corrupted classification accuracy when models are trained on clean labels, corrupted labels, or both?
Why is the MNIST result nearly invariant to kappa if spectral frequency is the operative mechanism?
Can phase-aware Fourier error, bandwise complex error, and boundary-robust bases replace clipped amplitude-ratio heatmaps?
How do accuracy, memory, and wall time scale with input dimension on the same controlled target family?
Can a versioned environment, fixed entrypoints, raw seed metrics, and figure-regeneration scripts reproduce every table and panel?
reusable_insights: Treat MGDL first as stage-wise residual optimization; only attach a spectral interpretation after measuring spectra in both original and learned feature coordinates.
Ablate independent residual ensembles, feature composition, freezing, grade summation, restarts, and final end-to-end fine-tuning separately.
Match methods by parameters, optimizer steps, FLOPs, peak memory, and wall time; report all of them because shallow frozen backprop changes their relationship.
Compare against direct frequency encodings and activations, not only an end-to-end ReLU network, on every spectral-bias benchmark.
Report complex Fourier coefficient error or power error without clipping and test sensitivity to windowing, periodic extension, and basis choice.
Use many seeds and publish the full distribution, especially when model selection ranges differ between methods.
Separate interpolation from memorization in coordinate regression by excluding train pixels from test metrics and reserving a validation grid.
Sum all grade times before comparing multi-stage training with one-shot baselines.
Distinguish learning high-frequency corruption from being robust to it; use both noisy-target and clean-target metrics plus task accuracy.
Use controlled target families across dimensions to support scaling claims rather than changing the task at high dimension.
Make the monotone-residual theorem operational by reporting achieved versus optimal grade loss and optimizer failure rates.
Release one configuration object shared by paper, code, and tests so commented research defaults cannot drift from executable defaults.
failure_modes: Early frozen features can discard information needed by later residuals, leaving no shallow output map able to recover the target.
Later grades can overfit residual noise while monotonically improving training MSE.
A large gain can arise from restart-and-boosting effects rather than composition, making the proposed explanation false even when the method works.
Frequency content can be low in one learned coordinate and high in another, making grade labels coordinate-dependent.
Four or five optimization stages can hide a much larger data-pass or update budget behind similar wall time on one hardware/software stack.
Tuning methods on different hyperparameter outcomes can create apparent architecture gains without a nested validation protocol.
Clipped amplitude ratios can show an overshooting, wrong-phase component as perfectly recovered.
Full-image PSNR can improve primarily by fitting included training pixels rather than interpolating unseen coordinates.
A method that ignores oscillatory label noise can be mischaracterized as one that successfully learned high frequencies.
Single-seed runs can conceal instability, especially at grade transitions where Figures 14-15 show loss spikes.
Frozen stage-wise training can underperform end-to-end learning when tasks require coordinated feature revision.
The current repository entrypoints can fail before training or silently run hundreds of times fewer epochs than the paper.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a novel sum-composition strategy, implemented through MGDL, in which shallow networks each learn low-frequency information and their compositions recover high-frequency components, thereby offering an easy, scalable, dimension-independent solution to DNN spectral bias.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The grade-wise residual/frozen-feature algorithm is clearly specified, and the synthetic and manifold tables show very large improvements over the same-depth end-to-end ReLU baseline with favorable reported time. Original-resolution figures show progressive recovery of higher original-coordinate frequencies, while the image and clean-label MNIST results suggest useful interpolation and regularization behavior.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Applying the earlier MGDL framework specifically to spectral-bias benchmarks and documenting progressive grade spectra is a meaningful empirical contribution. The proposed causal explanation is not established: no grade is frequency constrained, no internal-feature spectra are defined, the theory is only monotone residual fitting, and essential boosting/composition ablations are absent. Established frequency encodings, activations, filters, hash coordinates, and reparameterizations were already direct competitors but are omitted. The defensible novelty is therefore a strong proof of concept for stage-wise frozen-feature residual training against end-to-end ReLU, not a validated general solution to spectral bias or a state-of-field INR method.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Rahaman et al. establish low-frequency bias for ReLU networks and study how manifold complexity changes high-frequency expressivity. The reviewed paper reuses related synthetic and manifold setups but tests only its own grade-wise optimization against SGDL, so it does not independently delimit frequency definitions or the manifold effect.

competitive_landscape.title: A Phase Shift Deep Neural Network for High Frequency Approximation and Wave Problems
competitive_landscape.difference: PhaseDNN explicitly selects frequency bands, shifts each band to low frequency, learns it with a moderate network, and shifts it back, including Helmholtz examples. MGDL avoids explicit Fourier decomposition but never compares with this cited approach, so its convenience-versus-control tradeoff is unmeasured.

competitive_landscape.title: Multi-scale Deep Neural Networks for Solving High-Dimensional PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: MscaleDNN assigns input scales to subnetworks to cover a wide frequency range and evaluates high-dimensional PDEs. MGDL instead learns sequential residuals through frozen features; without a comparison, the paper cannot show that learned grade composition is preferable to explicit multiscale channels.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains
competitive_landscape.difference: Tancik et al. transform coordinates with tunable Fourier features and connect the result to a stationary NTK bandwidth, directly targeting image-coordinate regression. The reviewed paper cites it and uses the same task type but provides no Fourier-feature comparison, leaving its image advantage relative to the established solution unknown.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: SIREN uses sinusoidal activations and principled initialization to represent fine signal detail and derivatives across images, audio, video, and PDEs. MGDL retains ReLU and changes the training topology, but does not test whether its gains survive against a backbone designed for oscillatory functions.

competitive_landscape.title: Multiplicative Filter Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: MFNs multiply sinusoidal or Gabor filters applied to the input and admit an explicit exponentially large basis interpretation, largely matching or outperforming Fourier-feature and sinusoidal INRs in their study. This is more directly tied to frequency synthesis than MGDL's unconstrained learned compositions and should be a primary mechanism baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: BACON: Band-limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation
competitive_landscape.difference: BACON has an analytically controlled Fourier spectrum and produces supervised or unsupervised outputs at multiple scales. MGDL's grade spectra are observed after training rather than guaranteed, so BACON is a strong comparator for the claim that progressive composition yields interpretable frequency stages.

competitive_landscape.title: Residual Multiplicative Filter Networks for Multiscale Reconstruction
competitive_landscape.difference: Residual MFNs add skip connections and stage-wise initialization to preserve coarse structure while fitting finer frequency support. They combine residual stages with explicit spectral control, making them especially useful for distinguishing MGDL's residual-learning benefit from its frozen learned composition.

competitive_landscape.title: WIRE: Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: WIRE uses complex Gabor wavelet activations and reports accuracy, speed, and noise robustness across fitting and inverse tasks. MGDL has no explicit spatial localization or noise study, so WIRE is a direct image and robustness baseline omitted from the evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: DINER: Disorder-Invariant Implicit Neural Representation
competitive_landscape.difference: DINER learns a hash-table remapping that reorganizes discrete signals into an easier coordinate distribution and tests MLP and SIREN backbones across image, video, and inverse problems. It can sacrifice ordinary interpolation semantics, whereas MGDL preserves continuous input coordinates; a held-out-coordinate comparison would expose that tradeoff.

competitive_landscape.title: FINER: Flexible Spectral-bias Tuning in Implicit NEural Representation by Variable-periodic Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: FINER tunes the supported frequency set through a variable-periodic activation and bias initialization, with image, signed-distance, and radiance-field tests. It predates the reviewed submission and directly contests claims of an effective general spectral-bias solution, yet is absent from baselines and related work.

competitive_landscape.title: Improved Implicit Neural Representation with Fourier Reparameterized Training
competitive_landscape.difference: FR-INR reparameterizes MLP weights in fixed Fourier bases, analyzes frequency-gradient and NTK effects, and applies the change across several existing INR backbones. Unlike MGDL it leaves the architecture topology intact and supplies a mechanism analysis; direct matched tests would separate parameterization from stage-wise optimization.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards the Spectral bias Alleviation by Normalizations in Coordinate Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Cai et al. connect coordinate-network normalization to a more balanced NTK eigenvalue distribution and test broad inverse and representation tasks. This provides both a simpler intervention and a direct theory-led baseline that the reviewed paper's SGDL-only comparison lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: Computational Advantages of Multi-Grade Deep Learning: Convergence Analysis and Performance Insights
competitive_landscape.difference: Fang and Xu later analyze gradient-descent convergence, learning-rate robustness, and iterative Jacobian eigenvalues for image regression, denoising, and deblurring. This strengthens the optimization interpretation of MGDL, but it is a later same-lineage study and does not retroactively supply the target paper's missing frequency-band theorem or competitor/ablation controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Escaping Spectral Bias without Backpropagation: Fast Implicit Neural Representations with Extreme Learning Machines
competitive_landscape.difference: ELM-INR partitions the domain, solves random-feature local models by linear least squares, and adaptively refines regions using spectral Barron complexity. It attacks both spectral bias and iterative optimization cost, providing a current alternative to MGDL's multiple backpropagated grades.

competitive_landscape.title: Content-Aware Frequency Encoding for Implicit Neural Representations with Fourier-Chebyshev Features
competitive_landscape.difference: CAFE uses parallel learned projections and Hadamard products to synthesize and select a much larger frequency set in the encoding stage, with a Fourier-Chebyshev extension for stability. It directly operationalizes the composition-generates-frequencies intuition with explicit basis analysis and broad INR benchmarks rather than post-hoc grade spectra.

reviewer_notes: Primary audit covered all 19 pages of the canonical arXiv v1 PDF, including Equations 1-15, Theorem 1, Tables 1-4, Figures 1-15, every axis, legend, caption, colorbar, appendix, and all 49 references at original resolution. The official source archive was inspected and contains TeX plus raw figure assets. The linked implementation at https://github.com/Ronglong-Fang/AddressingSpectralBiasviaMGDL was audited at commit 6fafb66f039269a3592590bd0ab500ff8bc9f1c5 (2025-05-01): syntax compilation succeeds, but multiple entrypoints have undefined variables; paper-scale epoch counts are merely commented alternatives to much smaller defaults; results directories, tests, environment metadata, license, checkpoints, and raw metrics are absent; analysis files include absolute author paths. The image split and full-grid evaluation were independently confirmed in code. Competitor research used primary arXiv, OpenReview/ICLR, and CVF records checked through 2026-08-23. Interpretive claims deliberately preserve the substantial synthetic optimization result while separating it from unsupported claims of explicit band decomposition, dimension independence, and field-level superiority.
